q: Did games with smaller crowds coincide with smaller national TV audiences in 2025 and 2026?
report:
Yes on the raw numbers: comparing games on the same network, smaller crowds went with smaller national TV audiences (correlation 0.34 in 2025, n = 82, range 0.14 to 0.52; 0.47 in 2026, n = 83, range 0.29 to 0.62)[1]. Mostly no after comparing each game with its own park's usual crowd, so popular teams do not drive the result: the correlation falls to 0.16 in 2025 (range -0.05 to 0.37) and 0.14 in 2026 (range -0.08 to 0.34), and both ranges include zero[2]. Across team-seasons, teams with bigger average crowds also had bigger average national TV audiences (correlation 0.52, n = 56, range 0.30 to 0.69), which is consistent with team-level factors such as popularity and market size driving both, though the data does not prove the cause[3].

*Viewership figures are publicly reported and may differ from official Nielsen data. They are the national TV audience, excluding streaming add-ons. Nielsen changed its method on September 1, 2025, so 2025 and 2026 figures are not like-for-like. These are associations, not cause and effect.*

q: What drives MLB attendance?
report:
Major League Baseball attendance is strongest during home openers, weekend games, matchups against popular opponents, and seasons when the home team is winning or has a strong history of drawing crowds[1]. At the game level, home openers coincide with the largest positive difference, showing a 69.1% higher attendance compared to normal games[1]. Opponent matchups also relate to attendance: games against the Los Angeles Dodgers go with a 25.0% higher crowd, the New York Yankees with a 15.7% higher crowd, and the Chicago Cubs with a 13.1% higher crowd compared to an average opponent[1]. Conversely, weekday games go with lower attendance than Friday games, with Monday games showing a 21.8% lower crowd, Wednesdays 20.6% lower, Tuesdays 18.9% lower, and Thursdays 16.6% lower[1]. Early season timing also accompanies smaller crowds, as March and April games show a 10.9% lower attendance compared to August[1]. At the team level, a season win rate that is .100 higher goes with an 8.6% higher attendance, while a 10.0% higher average crowd over the prior two years goes with an 8.2% higher attendance[1]. Meanwhile, a 10.0% larger metro population goes with only a 0.2% higher attendance after accounting for prior crowds, which is an unclear relationship[1]. These patterns are reflected in models analyzing 7,205 games and 86 team-seasons across the 2024 to 2026 seasons[2].

*These are associations, not cause and effect.*

q: How did Cubs attendance change by month in 2025?
report: During the 2025 season, the Chicago Cubs' average home attendance and average fill rate rose through the spring to peak in June, then declined steadily through September[1]. In April, total home attendance was 474,334, with an average attendance of 33,881 and an average fill rate of 82.0%[1]. In May, total attendance reached 513,185, as the average attendance grew by 2,775 to an average of 36,656, and the average fill rate increased by 6.7 percentage points to 88.8%[1]. June saw total attendance at 395,310, while average attendance peaked at 39,531 (an increase of 2,875) and the average fill rate reached a high of 95.7%, up 7.0 percentage points[1]. In July, total attendance was 471,413, but average attendance fell by 247 to an average of 39,284, and the average fill rate dropped by 0.6 percentage points to 95.1%[1]. August total attendance was 535,022, while average attendance decreased by 1,069 to an average of 38,216, and the average fill rate fell by 2.6 percentage points to 92.6%[1]. Finally, September total attendance was 543,987, but average attendance declined by 1,950 to an average of 36,266, and the average fill rate dropped by 4.7 percentage points to 87.8%[1].

sources.query: WITH weekday_agg AS ( SELECT weekday, AVG(attendance) AS avg_attendance, AVG(expected_attendance) AS avg_expected_attendance, AVG(fill_pct) AS avg_fill_pct FROM games_clean WHERE season = 2025 GROUP BY weekday ), ordered AS ( SELECT weekday, avg_attendance, avg_expected_attendance, avg_fill_pct, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY avg_attendance DESC) as rn FROM weekday_agg ) SELECT weekday, avg_attendance, avg_expected_attendance, avg_fill_pct, LAG(avg_attendance) OVER (ORDER BY avg_attendance DESC) as prev_avg_attendance, avg_attendance - LAG(avg_attendance) OVER (ORDER BY avg_attendance DESC) as difference FROM weekday_agg ORDER BY avg_attendance DESC;

data_note: Data sources: MLB Stats API (statsapi.mlb.com).

q: Compare actual and expected average attendance for the five AL East teams in 2025.

chart.title: Actual and expected attendance by team name

report:
In 2025, the Boston Red Sox were the only AL East team to exceed their expected average attendance, while the New York Yankees, Toronto Blue Jays, and Baltimore Orioles all fell short, and the Tampa Bay Rays had no expected baseline because they played in a temporary stadium[1][2][3]. Specifically, the Red Sox actual average attendance of 34,278 was 354 higher than their expected average of 33,923, with a 90.8% fill rate[2]. Meanwhile, the Yankees actual average of 42,390 was 784 below their expected average of 43,174, with a 91.1% fill rate[2]. The Blue Jays actual average of 35,184 was 1,882 below their expected average of 37,066, with an 89.9% fill rate[2]. The Orioles actual average of 22,702 was 3,003 below their expected average of 25,706, with a 49.9% fill rate[2]. Finally, the Rays actual average attendance was 9,713 with an 88.1% fill rate, but their expected average is unknown because they were excluded from the model due to playing at Steinbrenner Field, a temporary park[2].

*Promotions are not in the data. These are associations, not cause and effect.*

sources.query: SELECT * FROM team_season_model WHERE team_id = 139 AND season = 2025
rows: Rays at Steinbrenner Field, a temporary park

sources.query: SELECT t.name AS team_name, ts.avg_attendance, ts.expected_avg_attendance, (ts.avg_attendance - ts.expected_avg_attendance) AS difference, ts.residual_pct, (SELECT avg(g.fill_pct) FROM games_clean g WHERE g.home_team_id = ts.team_id AND g.season = 2025) AS avg_fill_pct FROM team_season_model ts JOIN teams t ON ts.team_id = t.team_id AND ts.season = t.season WHERE t.division = 'American League East' AND ts.season = 2025 ORDER BY ts.avg_attendance DESC;

q: Rank the networks by average national TV audience in 2026.
report:
In 2026, Fox topped the national TV audience rankings with an average of 2,343,875 viewers across 24 windows, followed by Netflix with an average of 2,314,000 viewers for its 2 games, and NBC with an average of 2,312,762 viewers across 21 games[1]. ABC ranked fourth, averaging 1,794,333 viewers over 3 games[1]. ESPN followed with an average of 1,126,208 viewers across 24 games with known audiences, out of 27 total broadcasts[1]. TBS averaged 614,900 viewers across 10 games with known audiences out of 25 broadcasts, and FS1 finished last with an average of 385,905 viewers across 21 games with known audiences out of 39 broadcasts[1].

*Viewership figures are publicly reported and may differ from official Nielsen data. They are the national TV audience, excluding streaming add-ons.*

sources.query: SELECT network, average_viewers, broadcasts, network_text FROM network_audience WHERE season = 2026 ORDER BY average_viewers DESC
rows: Fox averaged 2,343,875 viewers across 24 windows with known audiences in 2026.
Netflix averaged 2,314,000 viewers across 2 games with known audiences in 2026.
NBC averaged 2,312,762 viewers across 21 games with known audiences in 2026.
